clue.text: Frequent public house

blocks.note: common land is public, shared by all
someone's place is their house, as in 'come round to my place'

explanation.surface: Someone describes their regular local pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frequent' reads as a verb (to frequent a pub) but is the adjective meaning occurring often.
explanation.definitionFit: Something commonplace is ordinary and often met with, so frequent in the sense of everyday and usual.

clue.text: Contemptible fellow importing Ecstasy

indicators.note: to import is to bring something inside, so one word takes another into its middle

blocks.note: a chap is a man or fellow
E is the street abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A despised man is caught bringing in drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Importing' reads as smuggling in the surface; here it only puts one piece inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap behaviour is mean and unworthy, a common synonym for contemptible or despicable.

clue.text: One may help one get a better image

definitions.text: One may help one get a better image

blocks.clueFragment: One may help one get a better image
blocks.note: surface reading: something like a stylist or PR adviser improves a person's public reputation
setter's reading: a lens that makes what you look at appear larger and clearer

explanation.surface: An image consultant polishes a client's public persona.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Image' suggests reputation; read literally it is the picture seen through a lens.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand-held lens enlarges small print or objects, so the viewer gets a bigger, clearer view.

clue.text: Its members should know the score

definitions.text: Its members should know the score

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom meaning to understand how things really stand
setter's reading: musicians who read from a written score of music

explanation.surface: A club or organisation expects its members to be well informed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Know the score' is an idiom for being worldly-wise; here a score is printed music.
explanation.definitionFit: A symphony ensemble's players all perform from the conductor's full score of the piece.

clue.text: The plant associated with Blakeney?

blocks.note: surface reading: a flower growing near Blakeney, a village on the Norfolk coast
setter's reading: Sir Percy Blakeney, hero of Baroness Orczy's novel, whose secret identity is named after a red wildflower

explanation.surface: A botanist asks which plant grows around Blakeney, a Norfolk village.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Percy Blakeney is the Scarlet Pimpernel, the hero who rescues aristocrats from the French Revolution in Orczy's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarlet pimpernel is a small red-flowered wild plant that gave Blakeney's alter ego its name.

clue.text: Book, in the end reduced

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so the phrase loses its final letter

blocks.note: 'at last' means finally, in the end

explanation.surface: A book is eventually cut down in length.
explanation.walkthrough: AT LAST loses its final T. An atlas is a book of maps.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound volume of maps, so it is a kind of book.

clue.text: Novelist could make fortune penning one after end of course

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept
to pen something is to enclose it, as an animal in a pen

blocks.note: the final letter of course
one's lot is one's fate or fortune
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A writer might make a fortune from one book after a course ends.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot, author of Middlemarch, is the pen name of Mary Ann Evans.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot, pen name of Mary Ann Evans, was a major Victorian novelist.

clue.text: Spring from rafter? Not quite

indicators.note: not quite all of the word is used, so its last letter falls away

blocks.note: a spar is a pole or beam, like a rafter

explanation.surface: Someone almost leaps from a roof beam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like a verb, jumping off the rafter; it is a mineral water source.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a mineral spring, or a resort built around one.

clue.text: Instructions produced since trio recast

indicators.note: to recast is to remould or reshape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to stage a play is to produce it
these nine letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions were written once a trio of performers changed its line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The D at the end of STAGED doubles as the start of the second word, so the jumble supplies only IRECTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage directions are the instructions in a script telling actors where to move and what to do.

clue.text: Almost lost governor in Russian city

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: to go astray is to get lost
a khan is a ruler or governor in Central Asia

explanation.surface: A regional governor nearly goes missing in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost' is an adjective here, wandering off course rather than mislaid.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrakhan is a port city on the Volga delta in southern Russia, also known for its curly lambskin.

clue.text: For example, it may be served with piece of gammon

definitions.text: For example, it may be served with piece of gammon

indicators.note: a piece is just a small part, here the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
the first letter of gammon

explanation.surface: A breakfast menu suggests something to go with ham.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer too: gammon and egg is a classic British pub dish. Gammon is cured ham.
explanation.definitionFit: A fried egg is the usual accompaniment to a gammon steak, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: One bringing an action in court about flat in country

indicators.note: in places one thing inside the other, the land enclosing the flat terrain
about means around, so the legal abbreviation wraps the rest

blocks.note: CT is the standard abbreviation for court
Oman is a country on the Arabian peninsula
a plain is flat land

explanation.surface: A litigant sues over an apartment abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two nested insertions, the court abbreviation wrapping the country, which wraps the level ground. 'Flat' suggests an apartment; it is level ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A complainant is the plaintiff, the party who brings a lawsuit against another.

clue.text: Of incalculable value, diamonds left in cupboard

indicators.note: in puts the first pair of items inside the piece of furniture

blocks.note: ice is slang for diamonds
L is the abbreviation for left
a press is a cupboard, especially for linen

explanation.surface: Valuable diamonds have been left in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' for a cupboard is chiefly British and Irish, as in a linen press. 'Left' is not a verb but the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something priceless is so valuable that no sum could be put on it.

clue.text: Greek character identified from epithet? Aristotle

indicators.note: identified from says the answer is picked out from within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a Greek figure can be identified by a nickname, perhaps Aristotle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person like Aristotle; it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, and a letter is a written character.

clue.text: Sob, drunk, by counter, and disparage one's own products

blocks.note: to sob is to cry
'stinking' is slang for very drunk
a fish is a gaming counter, a token used in card games

explanation.surface: A weeping drunk at a shop counter runs down the goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' just places one piece next to the next. A fish as a counter is an old sense, from gaming tokens shaped like fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry stinking fish is an idiom for belittling your own wares, like a fishmonger calling his stock rotten.

clue.text: Face irate criminal in self-service restaurant

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so these letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An angry offender causes a scene in a canteen.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafeteria is a restaurant where customers collect their own food from a counter.

clue.text: No decline, possibly, in sloth

indicators.note: possibly says these letters are one possible arrangement among others

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Laziness might mean things never get worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sloth' may suggest the animal; here it is the vice of laziness.
explanation.definitionFit: Indolence is habitual laziness, the same idle vice as sloth.

clue.text: Piece written about one standing over grave, having lost son (legendary character)

indicators.note: written about means set down around something, so one word encloses another
losing the son drops the letter that abbreviates son
in a down clue, standing over means placed above, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: piece is slang for a gun
I is the Roman numeral for one
grave and severe both mean serious

explanation.surface: A writer describes a mourner at a graveside who has lost a son.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the standard abbreviation for son. 'Grave' is the adjective meaning serious, not a burial place.
explanation.definitionFit: Guinevere is King Arthur's queen in Arthurian legend, lover of Lancelot.

clue.text: Bird deafening a pilot, when flying

indicators.note: flying suggests things scattered through the air and landing in a new order

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A bird strike deafens a pilot in mid-air.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan-tailed pigeon is a fancy breed of domestic pigeon with a spread, fan-shaped tail.

clue.text: Difficult and problematic drunk

blocks.note: first meaning: hard to get out of
second meaning: informal for intoxicated

explanation.surface: A drinker becomes awkward and troublesome.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight describes a hard, constricted situation and is also everyday slang for being tipsy.

clue.text: Jobs — first of tinkers seeks information

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of tinkers
to ask is to seek information

explanation.surface: A travelling repairman asks around for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jobs' sounds like employment the tinkers want; it is just tasks.
explanation.definitionFit: Jobs and tasks are both pieces of work to be done.

clue.text: Cartoon cat — terribly sly match, by the sound of it

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly, so the letters come out jumbled
says the word is matched by how it is said, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: these three letters rearranged
a vesta is a short wax match; in a non-rhotic accent it sounds the same as these letters

explanation.surface: A sly cartoon cat is a terrible match for its rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Vesta was a brand and general name for small matches; to British ears it sounds like the end of the cat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvester is the Looney Tunes cat forever chasing Tweety Pie.

clue.text: Father given new alarm

blocks.note: a sire is a father, especially of an animal
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A father receives a new alarm clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is a loud warning device, so an alarm.

clue.text: Runs over friend in motoring event

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A driver runs over a friend during a motor race.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'over' just places R above ALLY. 'Runs over' reads as a hit-and-run.
explanation.definitionFit: A rally is a long-distance motor race on public or rough roads.

clue.text: Comfort found by Saracen? Sure, in the wars

indicators.note: something in the wars has been knocked about, so the letters are battered into a new order

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Saracen fighting the Crusades finds solace.
explanation.walkthrough: Saracen was the medieval name for a Muslim opponent of the Crusaders, hence the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Reassurance is the comfort of having doubts or fears removed.

clue.text: Bird, domesticated one with head chopped off

indicators.note: chopping off the head removes the opening letter

blocks.note: fowl are domesticated birds such as chickens

explanation.surface: A tame bird has been beheaded for the pot.
explanation.definitionFit: The owl is a nocturnal bird of prey.

clue.text: Pompous person in gas station

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A self-important man holds forth at a petrol station.
explanation.definitionFit: An ass is a foolish person, often a pompous, self-important one.

clue.text: Be aware of Dutch painter going round steamship for no reason

indicators.note: going round means encircling, so the painter's name wraps the next item

blocks.note: to sense something is to be aware of it
Sir Peter Lely, Dutch-born portrait painter at the court of Charles II
SS is the prefix for steamship

explanation.surface: A painter circles a steamship without knowing why.
explanation.walkthrough: Lely was court painter to Charles II, a favourite crossword painter along with Etty and Hals.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something senselessly means doing it without purpose or reason.
